planting.note: Set rooted stem cuttings into a chunky, well-draining aroid mix in spring and give the vine a moss pole or bark totem to climb for the best leaf size and color.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light with high humidity and a loose, bark-based potting mix that drains quickly but never dries out completely between waterings. Philodendron andreanum is a climbing aroid native to the forests of Colombia and Ecuador, prized for its elongated, heart-shaped leaves that emerge thin and pale before deepening into a velvety, near-black green crossed with pale silvery-green veining that stands out sharply against the dark blade. As a true climbing species it should be trained upright on a support rather than left to trail, since vertical growth encourages larger, more dramatically colored mature leaves. Keep it out of direct sun, which scorches the velvety cuticle, and avoid temperatures below 55F. All parts are toxic if ingested due to calcium oxalate crystals.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew) — Philodendron andreanum

planting.note: Mount or pot rooted cuttings in a coarse, fast-draining aroid mix and let the plant climb or hang; it tolerates drying out between waterings better than many thin-leaved philodendrons.

directions: Give this species bright, filtered light and a chunky, quick-draining substrate, allowing the top layer to dry before watering again. Philodendron crassinervium is a hemiepiphytic species from southeastern Brazil named for the noticeably thick, raised midrib running down its narrow, elongated, leathery leaves, a feature that distinguishes it from thinner-leaved philodendron relatives at a glance. It climbs or scrambles over host trees in habit and adapts well to being grown as a trailing or climbing houseplant on a pole or in a hanging basket. Its leathery foliage makes it noticeably more tolerant of brief dry spells and lower humidity than velvet-leaved collector philodendrons. All parts are toxic if chewed or ingested.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew) — Philodendron crassinervium

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or cuttings in a rich, well-drained potting mix in part shade and give the self-heading plant room to spread as it matures into a large, multi-trunked specimen.

directions: Grow in part shade to bright, filtered light in a humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-draining soil, watering regularly during active growth and reducing in cooler months. Philodendron angustisectum is a large, self-heading tropical aroid native to Ecuador and Peru, closely resembling the familiar tree philodendron but distinguished by its more deeply and finely divided, narrow-lobed leaf segments, giving the foliage a lacier, more feathery appearance. As it matures it develops a thick, sometimes multi-stemmed trunk and prominent aerial roots, eventually forming an imposing architectural specimen useful as a large understory or patio accent in warm climates. It is tolerant of a range of light levels once established but produces its most finely cut foliage in bright, indirect light. All parts are toxic if ingested due to calcium oxalate crystals.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew) — Philodendron angustisectum
